name: Sensitivity
seoDesc: Sensitivity: work out false negative from the true positive and the sensitivity. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the true positive, the sensitivity, the true negative and the specificity and the Sensitivity calculator solves for false negative. That makes it useful for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Editing anything puts the results away until the next press of Calculate — change one value at a time and the updated answer tells you what that value was worth.

sections.title: How does the Sensitivity calculator work?
sections.html:
The Sensitivity calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports false negative in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the true positive, the sensitivity, the true negative and the specificity.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Sensitivity calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

False negative=-true positive + true positive ÷ sensitivity
False positive=-true negative + true negative ÷ specificity
Positive likelihood ratio=-sensitivity ÷ (specificity − 1)
Negative likelihood ratio=(1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity
PPV=prevalence × sensitivity ÷ (prevalence × sensitivity + prevalence × specificity − prevalence − specificity + 1)
NPV=specificity × (prevalence − 1) ÷ (prevalence × sensitivity + prevalence × specificity − prevalence − specificity)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose True positive = 10 and Sensitivity = 10 %. Working through the relationship above gives False negative = 90.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: False negative = 90 should be roughly the size you expected from True positive = 10 and Sensitivity = 10 %.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Sensitivity calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the true positive, the sensitivity and the true negative — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Sensitivity calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns false negative, derived from the true positive, the sensitivity and the true negative. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Sensitivity calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the true positive, the sensitivity, the true negative and the specificity, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter sensitivity in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Sensitivity opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports False negative = 90. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Sensitivity calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
